# University College London (UCL) Summary
University College London (UCL), founded in 1826 as London University, was established as a secular alternative to Oxford and Cambridge, pioneering inclusivity by admitting students regardless of religious background. It quickly became a major academic institution in London, innovating by appointing the first science faculty head in Britain, introducing chairs in political economy and geography, and founding the first teaching hospital in 1834. In 1836, UCL was incorporated as University College, London under Royal Charter as part of the newly established federal University of London, gaining full university status in 2023.
UCL is based primarily in Bloomsbury, Central London, with its historic Wilkins Building and recent expansions including the UCL East campus at the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, opened in 2022–2023. It operates a broad estate with 26 halls of residence and has earned distinction for sustainability, recently ranking joint fifth globally for environmental impact. UCL is organized into eleven faculties and is a founding member of the Russell Group and the University of London, with strong affiliations internationally. Renowned for its research power, it operates numerous specialized centers and its open access press, UCL Press. UCL is consistently ranked in the top 25 global universities and was named the Times/Sunday Times Good University Guide’s University of the Year for 2024. Its diverse and highly international student body numbers over 46,000, with a majority of students from outside the UK and ongoing commitment to widening participation and social inclusion. UCL alumni and staff include 33 Nobel laureates and three Fields Medalists, reflecting its historic impact in research and education.
